questions.question: A company needs a fixed public IPv4 address for a single EC2 instance that must survive stop/start cycles. The instance is currently running with its default addressing. What should the architect do?
options: Assign an Elastic IP to the instance, since the default public IP can change on stop/start
Rely on the instance's public IP, since an EC2 public IP never changes after launch
Move the instance into a private network and connect to it via NAT and an internet gateway
Register the private IP in a DNS record, since private IPs are fixed for the instance lifetime
questions.explanation: An Elastic IP is a public IPv4 you own until you delete it, so it stays fixed across stop/start; the default public IP is not permanent, so option B is wrong; NAT plus internet gateway only gives private machines outbound WWW access and does not provide a fixed public address, so C is wrong; private IPs are not reachable from the internet, so D is wrong.

questions.question: A web tier behind a single stable entry point must scale to multiple instances, and the design should avoid scarce public addresses on the instances. Which solution best fits?
options: Allocate a public IP directly to every instance in the web tier
Front the instances with a Load Balancer and don't use a public IP on the instances
Attach one Elastic IP to each of the instances in the fleet
Attach a single Elastic IP to the whole fleet simultaneously
questions.explanation: The section recommends a Load Balancer with no public IP on the instances for a stable, scalable entry point; public IPs per instance are the brittle pattern being avoided, so A is wrong; Elastic IPs reflect poor architectural decisions and consume the 5-per-account limit, so C is wrong; an Elastic IP can be attached to only one instance at a time, so D is wrong.
questions.keyTopic: Avoid Elastic IP: DNS name or Load Balancer

questions.question: An application team wants a stable, human-facing endpoint for a web server without consuming an Elastic IP. What is the recommended approach?
options: Request an increase of the Elastic IP quota and attach one to the server
Recreate the instance each time the public IP changes to keep a fixed address
Use a random public IP and register a DNS name to it
Advertise the instance's private IP to external clients
questions.explanation: Registering a DNS name to a random public IP keeps a stable user-facing endpoint while hiding the changing public IP; raising the Elastic IP quota still uses a scarce Elastic IP that the section advises avoiding, so A is wrong; recreating instances is not a fix for address stability, so B is wrong; the private IP is not reachable from the internet, so D is wrong.
questions.keyTopic: Avoid Elastic IP: DNS name or Load Balancer

questions.question: A solutions architect has been asked to add a sixth Elastic IP address in one AWS account. What is the most accurate statement about this request?
options: The account already has 5 Elastic IPs; the limit can be increased by asking AWS
The account already has 5 Elastic IPs and the limit can never be increased
The limit is 5 per Region, so the request is automatically approved
The limit is 5 per instance, so the third instance can receive its own Elastic IP
questions.explanation: The section states you can have 5 Elastic IPs in your account and can ask AWS to increase that limit; option B contradicts the documented ability to request an increase; option C is a per-Region claim not made in the source; option D misstates the quota, which is per account, not per instance.
questions.keyTopic: Elastic IP limit of 5 per account

questions.question: An operations team reports that an instance's public IP changed after a stop and start. Which statement explains the underlying behaviour?
options: Public IPs are unique across the whole web, so they cannot change
Stopping and then starting an EC2 instance can change its public IP
Private IPs are renumbered by AWS on every stop and start
The Elastic IP was remapped to another instance automatically
questions.explanation: The section explicitly says stopping and then starting an instance can change its public IP; uniqueness across the web does not imply permanence, so A is wrong; the behaviour concerns the public IP, not the private one, so C is wrong; no Elastic IP is involved in a default-addressed instance, so D is wrong.

questions.question: Two different companies each build a private network and both choose the address 192.168.0.1/22. Which statement is correct?
options: This is a conflict; private IPs must be unique across the whole web
This is valid because only a specified range may be used as private IP but the value may repeat
This is valid only if the two networks are connected through NAT and an internet gateway
This is invalid because private IPs must be unique within each AWS account
questions.explanation: Private IPs only need to be unique inside their own private network, so two companies can reuse the same range, and private addressing is restricted to a specified range; option A confuses the public-IP rule with private addressing; option C is irrelevant to reuse; option D invents a per-account uniqueness rule for private IPs.

questions.question: A server on a private network needs to reach websites on the WWW. Its private IP is not routable from the internet. What mechanism provides that access?
options: A NAT with an internet gateway acting as a proxy
A public IP added directly to the server's network interface
An Elastic IP attached to the private network interface
A DNS name registered to the private IP address
questions.explanation: Machines with private IPs connect to the WWW using NAT plus an internet gateway, a proxy mechanism; option B would give the server a public address, which is not how private-to-WWW access is described; option C misuses an Elastic IP, which is a public IPv4 attached to one instance; option D cannot make a private IP routable on the internet.
questions.keyTopic: NAT and internet gateway for WWW access

questions.question: An administrator must SSH into a newly launched EC2 instance from a laptop outside AWS. The instance has both a private and a public IP. Which address should be used, and why?
options: The public IP, because the private IP is only unique within the private network and cannot be reached from outside
The private IP, because it is fixed and the public IP may change after a stop and start
The private IP, because SSH traffic is proxied by the internet gateway to that address
The public IP, because Elastic IPs are required for SSH access to any EC2 instance
questions.explanation: From outside AWS you can only SSH using the public IP because you are not in the same network as the private IP; option B is true about public IP changes but does not make the private IP reachable; option C is wrong because the internet gateway does not give an external client a route to the private address; option D is wrong because SSH does not require an Elastic IP, only a public IP.

questions.question: A production instance fails and the team needs traffic to move to a standby instance in the same account as quickly as possible. Which Elastic IP capability supports this?
options: Rapidly remap the Elastic IP to the standby instance
Attach the same Elastic IP to both instances at the same time
Recreate the instance so its default public IP is reassigned
Add the Elastic IP to a private network and route via NAT
questions.explanation: The section says an Elastic IP can mask the failure of an instance or software by rapidly remapping the address to another instance in your account; option B is impossible because an Elastic IP attaches to one instance at a time; option C does not provide a controlled failover address; option D is not how a private network plus NAT provides a public endpoint.
questions.keyTopic: Elastic IP attach to one instance

questions.question: A new EC2 instance is launched with default settings. Which addressing does it receive?
options: A private IP for the internal AWS Network and a public IP for the WWW
A public IP only, because public IPs are sufficient for internal AWS traffic
An Elastic IP, because public IPs are not assigned by default
A private IP only, because a public IP must be requested explicitly
questions.explanation: By default an EC2 machine comes with a private IP for the internal AWS Network and a public IP for the WWW; option B omits the default private IP; option C is wrong because an Elastic IP is optional and not the default; option D is wrong because the default launch does include a public IP.
